prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Coyote scruff in canyons off Mulholland Drive. Fragrance of sage and rosemary, now it’s spring. At night the mockingbirds ring their warnings of cats coming across the neighborhoods. Like castanets in the palms of a dancer, the palm trees clack. The HOLLYWOOD sign has a white skin of fog across it where erotic canyons hump, moisten, slide, dry up, swell, and shift. They appear impatient—to make such powerful contact with pleasure that they will toss back the entire cover of earth. She walks for days around brown trails, threading sometimes under the low branches of bay and acacia. Bitter flowers will catch her eye: pink and thin honeysuckle, or mock orange. They coat the branches like lace in the back of a mystical store. Other deviant men and women live at the base of these canyons, closer to the city however. Her mouth is often dry, her chest tight, but she is filled to the brim with excess idolatry. It was like a flat mouse—the whole of Los Angeles she could hold in the circle formed by her thumb and forefinger. Tires were planted to stop the flow of mud at her feet. But she could see all the way to Long Beach through a tunnel made in her fist. Her quest for the perfect place was only a symptom of the same infection that was out there, a mild one, but a symptom nonetheless.

In the spring, the canyons cascading off Mulholland Drive awaken into a vibrant, living landscape. The air hums with a rich sensory soundscape—the territorial calls of mockingbirds, the dry clacking of palm fronds shifting in the breeze, and the elusive Yip-calls of coyotes moving unseen through the native flora. Higher up, shrouded in a dense, creeping fog, the hills surrounding the iconic HOLLYWOOD sign take on a surreal quality. The earth itself seems to physically shift and swell beneath the mist, breathing with an intense, sensual energy that blurs the boundary between the natural world and myth.

Winding her way along the narrow canyon trails, a solitary woman pushes through patches of bitter wildflowers. The ascent demands real physical strain, her muscles aching against the steep incline, but the physical toll is accompanied by a weight of a different kind: an overwhelming sensation of excess idolatry. Surrounded by the lingering ghosts of fame, fantasy, and manufactured magic, the trail feels heavy with the projected desires of millions, turning a simple hike into a walk through a sanctuary of modern icons.

Upon reaching an elevated ridge, the vast, chaotic expanse of Los Angeles unfolds below her. From this height, the sprawling metropolis suffers a sudden collapse of scale; the endless grid of streets and towers appears deceptively small, compact enough to frame neatly within the curve of her hand. Yet, this illusion of control offers no lasting stillness. Her persistent search for the perfect place—the ultimate vista, the ideal sanctuary—reveals itself not as an isolated desire, but as a symptom of a broader, mild infection that permeates the entire territory. It is a quiet, endemic restlessness shared by the land and its inhabitants alike, forever hunting for a perfection that remains just beyond the horizon.
outputs.L4:
It began as a low-frequency hum beneath her ribs—a persistent, tetherless ache that no quiet room or deliberate breathing could soothe. She called it a search for a sanctuary, a desperate craving for a singular, sacred patch of earth where the mind might finally come to rest. Driven by this quiet fever, she turned her back on the flat grid of the gridlocked streets and climbed into the wild, folded topography of the Los Angeles canyons.

For days, she walked. The city vanished behind sandstone outcroppings and reemerged as a distant, glittering rumor. She surrendered herself entirely to the rugged, sensory overload of the chaparral. Her boots kicked up clouds of fine, pale dust that settled into the creases of her skin. The air was a heavy, volatile perfume: the sharp, medicinal bite of crushed white sage, the sweet rot of fallen eucalyptus bark, and the sun-baked scent of dry sumac. 

She tracked the shifting microclimates of the hills. In the deep, shadowy ravines, damp oak canopies offered a cool, hushed respite where dry creek beds whispered of forgotten winter rains. Up on the exposed spines of the ridges, the heat was direct and punishing, radiating off pink granite boulders while the red-tailed hawks rode the warm updrafts overhead. Her feet grew calloused, her throat dry, but she pushed onward, climbing higher, convinced that around the next sharp switchback lay the stillness she had spent her life lacking.

On the afternoon of the fourth day, she reached a high, wind-scoured peak in the Santa Monicas. Below her, the canyon fell away into a sheer drop, opening up to a panoramic view of the vast Los Angeles basin. The air was remarkably clear, framed by the pale blue ocean on one side and the hazy wall of the San Gabriel mountains on the other. 

Standing on the edge, she raised her right hand toward the horizon. By bringing her thumb and forefinger together, she found she could visually manipulate the scale of the world. She squeezed the soaring downtown skyscrapers until they were no bigger than a cluster of gray pebbles. She pinched the endless, crawling ribbons of the freeway system into tiny, dark threads. The immense, overwhelming metropolis—a place of nine million souls, endless noise, and crushing ambition—was rendered harmless, shrunk to the size of her own palm. 

For a brief second, she felt a wave of triumph. But as the wind whipped past her ears, the sensation dissolved, leaving behind a cold, sudden clarity. 

She looked at her dusty boots, then down at the miniaturized landscape framing her fingers. The sanctuary she was looking for did not exist on this peak, nor in the deep canyons, nor anywhere beyond them. Her relentless impulse to wander—this burning need to climb, to escape, to conquer, to find something better just over the next ridge—was not the cure for her affliction. It *was* the affliction. 

And it was the exact same hunger that had built the city below. Los Angeles was a monument to restless dreamers, a sprawling desert mirage carved out by people who had run out of continent, forever chasing an ideal that kept shifting just out of reach. She had not left the city behind at all. Up here on the lonely, windblown ridge, carrying her endless, unquenchable longing, she was the most Los Angeles thing in the world.
outputs.L5:
High above the shimmering, endless grid of Los Angeles, Mulholland Drive snakes along the spine of the Santa Monica Mountains. It is a legendary stretch of asphalt, steeped in cinematic history, late-night mysteries, and the quiet glitz of the hillside mansions clinging to the cliffs. By day, it offers tourist-poster views of the city; by night, it becomes a dark ribbon of territory where the boundary between urban sprawl and raw wilderness completely dissolves.

It is in these late, quiet hours that the true master of the ridge appears. 

Rounding a tight, moonlit curve, a driver’s headlights cut through the gloom, catching a pair of amber eyes glowing in the darkness. Standing on the double yellow line is a lone coyote. Unflinching in the glare of the high beams, the creature pauses, perfectly still. Its lean, grey-brown coat blends seamlessly with the surrounding chaparral, a silent ghost of the native landscape. 

In a city built on ambition, reinvention, and fleeting fame, the coyote represents a very different kind of success: pure survival. Long before the road was paved, and long before the valley below burned bright with millions of neon lights, its ancestors hunted these exact canyon slopes. Today, while the world changes around it, the coyote simply adapts. It navigates the manicured lawns of million-dollar estates and the dangerous curves of the road with equal, indifferent grace. 

For a brief, suspended moment, two worlds intersect on Mulholland Drive—the quiet pulse of untamed nature meeting the hum of a modern machine. The coyote gives a final, assessing glance toward the windshield, entirely unbothered by the human intruder. Then, with a fluid, shadow-like leap, it slips over the guardrail and vanishes into the dark brush of the canyon, leaving the road once again to the night wind and the distant, twinkling city lights below.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of atmospheric literary fiction about a woman wandering the trails around Mulholland Drive in spring. Focus on vivid sensory details of LA flora, wildlife, and the urban landscape.
counterfactuals.output:
The air at four o’clock smelled of sun-baked resin, crushed black sage, and the sharp, medicinal tang of eucalyptus drifting up from the canyons. 

Mira walked the narrow dirt spine above Mulholland, where the mountain dropped away into two distinct worlds. To her left, the San Fernando Valley lay flat and blinding under the late April sun, a mosaic of white stucco, pale roofs, and shimmering asphalt. To her right, the Los Angeles basin unfurled toward the ocean, swallowed in a soft lavender smog that blurred the downtown scrapers into ghostly monoliths.

Spring had been violent with rain weeks ago, and now the chaparral was wild with the hangover of it. Thick strands of invasive wild mustard towered over her shoulders, their yellow petals so bright they seemed to vibrate against the dull ochre of the earth. She brushed past them, leaving a smear of buttery pollen across the sleeve of her linen shirt. Beneath the mustard, low bushes of ceanothus—California lilac—foamed in bursts of electric, hazy blue, humming with wild bees.

The dirt beneath her sneakers was dry, fine as flour, puffing up in tiny clouds with every step. A western fence lizard, its belly a flash of startling turquoise, froze on a chunk of exposed sandstone, its throat pulsing before it darted into the dry chamise.

Mira stopped at a high turnout where the fire road narrowed into a deer path. The wind pulled at her hair, carrying the low, oceanic roar of the 405 freeway thousands of feet below—a continuous sound, like blood rushing through a giant vein. Out here, the noise of ten million people was reduced to a soft, metallic thrumming, easily punctured by the sharp, scolding bark of a scrub jay hidden in a coast live oak.

High above, a red-tailed hawk rode an invisible thermal, suspended in the pale sky like a dark kite. Its shadow swept silently over the hillside, crossing over the jagged white teeth of yucca blossoms and the rusted frame of a forgotten 1970s sedan half-buried in the scrub, long devoured by rust and morning glory vines.

As the sun began its slow dip toward the Pacific, the light turned heavy and golden, thick as syrup. The swimming pools tucked into the folds of Bel Air glittered like dropped pieces of glass. A cool breeze pushed up through the canyon, carrying the damp smell of oak leaf mold and the faint, sweet perfume of night-blooming jasmine waking up in the terraced gardens below.

Mira sat on a flat outcrop of rock, her hands resting on her knees. A hundred yards down the slope, at the edge of the shadow line, the dry brush crackled. She held her breath. A coyote emerged—lean, silver-grey, its coat dusted with yellow mustard pollen. It didn't look at her. It moved with fluid, ghost-like grace across the ridge, pausing only once to test the wind before slipping into the deep violet shadows of the canyon.

Below, the grid of the city began to ignite, street by street, bulb by bulb, a carpet of fallen stars spreading out toward an invisible sea. Mira stayed until the yellow hills turned grey, bound to the earth by the scent of warm dust and wild sage.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a descriptive excerpt in the poetic, sensual style of classic Los Angeles writers like Eve Babitz or Joan Didion, capturing the eerie, lush atmosphere of the LA canyons.
counterfactuals.output:
By six o’clock in July, the canyon stopped breathing and simply began to ferment. It was that syrupy, bruised twilight—the color of a black-eyed Susan left too long in the sun—where the light didn’t fall so much as it pooled in the overgrown ravines. Up here, suspended on a road that felt less like civil engineering and more like a temporary agreement with gravity, you could smell the whole city's secret life: the medicinal tang of eucalyptus peeling like sunburned skin, dry sage, and the heavy, almost erotic decay of night-blooming jasmine crawling over chain-link fences.

It was dangerously lush, a predatory kind of green that clung to cliffs always one Santa Ana wind away from catching fire, or one winter rain away from sliding into the Boulevard below. The silence up in the hills was never really quiet; it was thick and static-charged, heavy with the neurotic, high-pitched yapping of coyotes moving through the chaparral. Below us, the distant grid of Los Angeles hummed like a vast, electric ocean, glowing with a million tiny, cold lights. But up in the canyon, under the heavy canopy of bougainvillea and dark oak, it felt like being hidden inside a velvet pocket—beautiful, suffocating, and waiting for the inevitable spark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a character looking out over the entire expanse of Los Angeles from high up in the hills, blending sensory observations of native plants with her internal sense of restlessness and isolation.
counterfactuals.output:
Elena stood where the packed dirt trail gave way to a sheer, crumbling drop, the soles of her boots kicking loose a small avalanche of granite dust. High in the Santa Monica Mountains, the city did not feel like a home; it felt like an ancient, sun-baked basin that had been paved over while nobody was looking. 

Beneath her, Los Angeles unfurled to the horizon—an endless, indifferent grid of concrete and glass, suffocated beneath a bruised haze of smog and late-afternoon heat. Four million people were living out their tiny, urgent dramas down there, yet up here, the silence was vast and heavy. She felt completely, profoundly untethered, an alien watching a distant civilization through a warped lens.

A hot gust of Santa Ana wind swept up the canyon, carrying the sharp, medicinal tang of black sage. Elena reached down absently, snapping a dried blossom of California buckwheat between her thumb and forefinger. The petals crumbled instantly into a rust-colored powder. The native flora didn't fight the drought; it surrendered to it, parched and dormant, holding its breath until winter. She envied that patient stillness. Inside her own chest, a frantic, useless pulse hammered away. Her mind was a caged animal, pacing back and forth, desperate for a change she couldn't name and a connection she couldn't reach. 

She walked a few paces along the ridgeline, her hand brushing against the stiff, leathery leaves of a Toyon bush. Beside it, the long, dagger-like stalks of a *Yucca whipplei*—Our Lord’s Candle—thrust upward toward the washed-out sky, armed against the elements with fierce, defensive spines. Elena felt similarly prickly, coated in a layer of sweat and dirt, guarded against a city that promised intimacy but delivered only scale. 

From this height, the hum of the 405 freeway was reduced to a low, metallic murmur, like the sound of water trapped in a pipe. She watched a red tailed hawk ride a thermal above the canyon floor, effortless and entirely detached from the earth. 

Below, the afternoon light began to bleed out, shifting the city’s concrete skin from bleached bone to lavender, and finally to a murky indigo. One by one, the streetlights began to ignite, a sprawling constellation of yellow and white circuit boards stretching all the way to the ink-black void of the Pacific. 

Elena breathed in deeply, catching the musky, resinous scent of coastal sage scrub mixed with the faint, warm exhaust drifting up from the valley. Millions of glowing windows, millions of lives intersecting, yet she felt anchored to the quiet dirt, invisible to the world below. The mountain was holding her up, but it offered no answers—only the dry wind rustling through the scrub oak, and the maddening, beautiful expanse of a city she was in, but never truly of.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about the wild edge of Los Angeles—specifically the canyons below the Hollywood sign, coyotes at night, and the fog rolling in.
counterfactuals.output:
The city curls inward at midnight, but the canyons keep their mouths open, breathing in the dark. Up where the yellow dust of the trail gives way to brittle chaparral, the nine white letters loom like a broken fence between the glow of the dream factory and the ancient sleep of the mountain. Here, at the ragged hem of Los Angeles, the concrete loses its confidence. The air changes scent—from hot asphalt and exhaust to crushed sage, damp earth, and dry mustard weed waiting for a spark.

Then the Pacific sends its long, cool breath inland. The fog rolls over the crest line not as a cloud, but as a slow, heavy tide, creeping down the ravines and drowning the streetlights block by block. It fills the hollows below the Sign until the letters seem to float on a glowing sea of pearl, stripped of their history, reduced to cardboard cutouts fading into the gray. The grid of the flatlands vanishes. The hum of the freeway softens into a dull, oceanic surge. The world shrinks to the radius of a single streetlight wrapped in a wool sweater of mist.

Out of this damp extinction, the ghosts take their shape. They move without sound through the chain-link shadows and the dry creek beds—slender, gray-ribbed coyotes, their fur tipped with frost and dust. They are the true landlords of the slope. They walk the fine, trembling line where swimming pools meet snake-runs, amber eyes catching the faint blue backlight of living room windows. When one rises on a sandstone outcrop to lift its snout toward the obscured stars, its yip is a glass rod snapping in the cold. Then another answers from the darkness of Beachwood, and another from Bronson, a sudden, laughing choir that vibrates in the chest of the canyon. They sing to the sleeping mansions, to the forgotten paths, to the ocean buried under the cloud, reminding the city below that it is built on borrowed dirt, and that the hills are only waiting for the fog to clear so they can take it back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a story scene: A woman spends days walking the brown dirt trails of the Hollywood Hills. Include specific details like sage and rosemary, mockingbirds, palm trees clacking, holding the distant city in a circle made by her thumb and forefinger, and the feeling that her quest for a perfect place is a mild infection.
counterfactuals.output:
By the fifth afternoon, the pale, powdery dirt of the Hollywood Hills had worked its way into every crease of her leather boots and settled like dust beneath her fingernails. It was a stubborn, sun-baked dirt that rose in small clouds with every step, turning the hem of her linen trousers a dull, tawny brown.

She brushed against the overgrown borders of the narrow trail, her knuckles dragging through wild sage and tough, sun-baked rosemary. The plants released a sharp, resinous perfume that clung to her warm skin, masking the faint, metallic tang of her own sweat. Above her, high in the bleached branches of a dead eucalyptus, a mockingbird launched into a chaotic, brilliant soliloquy—shifting effortlessly from the squeak of a rusty gate to a car alarm, then to the sweet, liquid notes of a song it had borrowed from a stranger. 

A hot canyon breeze swept up from the ravine below, setting the tall, spindly fan palms into motion. They clacked together in the gust—a dry, wooden sound, like ribs knocking in the wind or venetian blinds falling shut in an empty room.

She paused at a rocky turnout where the earth plummeted into a steep, chaparral-covered chute. 

The impulse that had kept her marching these trails for days—this restless, roving quest for the *perfect* place, the exact geographic coordinate where her life might finally click into alignment—had begun to feel less like a calling and more like a mild infection. It wasn't a roaring fever that put her to bed, but a low-grade, persistent itch under the skin. A light, warm sweat behind her knees that never quite cooled. It was an inflammation of the imagination, a quiet delirium telling her that the perfect vantage point, the true sanctuary, lay just around the next dust-blind curve.

Mara stepped to the edge of the dirt ridge. Below her, the vast, shimmering grid of Los Angeles stretched out toward the ocean, swallowed by a layer of violet smog and afternoon heat. 

Slowly, she raised her right hand to her face. She curled her thumb to meet the tip of her forefinger, forming a neat, tiny circle of skin. Closing one eye, she brought the frame up to her sightline. She adjusted her hand until the distant, glass needles of Downtown, the crawling ribbons of the freeways, and miles of sunlit stucco were all contained within that small ring of bone and flesh. 

She held the vast, chaotic city inside her tiny circle, holding her breath, waiting to see if squeezing it into something manageable would finally make it feel like home. The palm trees clacked behind her. The mockingbird sang. After a long minute, her shoulder began to ache, and she let her hand drop back to her side, turning to face the next rising hill.
